ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 曰 opens the explicit unnamed questioner’s follow-up question; 師曰 opens Fushan Dexuan’s answer after the headword-bearing clause.
ActorAttribution.ReviewedBy: Codex Lane C position 22 full-case author

Senses.Explanation: To live and die together is to share the same exposure in a Chan encounter: the exact named speaker calls for someone who will stand with him through the case rather than remain a spectator. Dahui Zonggao asks whether anyone will live and die together with him, then calls that person out to meet his staff. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise asks for a patch-robed monk who will do so after raising Fengxue’s opposed alternatives. These are public challenges, not descriptions of two people sharing dates of birth and death. Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to the cited named speaker who enters the same cauldron and furnace as the person being freed, and elsewhere to going through the fire sermon with the buddhas of the three times. Yunwai Xingze uses it in a memorial address but immediately refuses to let the phrase pass without a further test. An unnamed monk asks Fushan Dexuan directly what living and dying together is; Fushan turns the question back on whether the explicit unnamed questioner may be called Buddha. The sources repeatedly mark shared exposure, accompaniment, or matched commitment under a live test. They do not make the phrase a promise of literal simultaneous death, nor do they supply one abstract theory behind every case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120) (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Huiyun Benchong Sheng. The full-case proof distinguishes this actor from nearby respondents, questioners, and section subjects.

Senses.Explanation: As a figure for speech, the tongue is said to lack bones, be cut off, or be restrained from moving in public exchange. A person's capacity to speak is what Chan verdicts test, trust, disable, or demand under the image of the tongue. Yungai Jipeng and Chengtian Weijian each answer a public question by saying that the tongue has no bone. Guanghui Yuanlian says that he no longer doubts the tongues of old masters, and Shoushan Xingnian immediately asks him to state his understanding. Huangbo Xiyun predicts that Linji Yixuan will cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. Longyuan Fa says that a demon king has cut off the Buddha's tongue and offers to redress the wrong. Huiyun Benchong Sheng orders a respondent to produce a statement without moving the tongue, then says the respondent's shout still involves lips and mouth. These are speech acts and verdicts, not reports of bodily injury, so they establish a Zen-loaded referent separate from the organ that can be bitten.

Senses.Note: Two independent bodily witnesses establish the ordinary anatomical referent. No special Zen deviation is asserted for it.

Senses.Explanation: A tongue dragging on the ground is speech made bodily excessive: the organ extends so far that it trails along the earth. Chan masters deploy the image as an answer about a saying, as Zhongfeng Mingben’s capping comment on a visitor’s words, and as a cost of choosing one side of a comparison. Wuzhun Shifan answers a question about Zhaozhou’s saying of no guest and host with “the tongue drags on the ground,” then answers the follow-up with “words fill the world.” Zhongfeng Mingben inserts the phrase after replaying a visitor’s answer “I came for the teaching.” Juelang Daosheng gives it as the answer requested before birth, then follows it with “eyebrows propping up heaven.” Mingjue Cong says that choosing Yunmen in his comparison would wrong himself until his tongue dragged on the ground.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X81/X81n1568.xml). Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (Vols. 10–25) (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)): Yungai Jipeng answers a direct question about the main point of the teaching with 'the tongue has no bone.'

Senses.Explanation: The tongue has no bone is a Chan appraisal of speech as able to turn without a rigid support: masters use it for agile wording, unreliable verbal flexibility, or a line that can be extended and reversed, so the saying can praise responsiveness or expose talk that bends too easily. Hongzhi Zhengjue pairs Shitou's boneless tongue with Yunmen's sinewed eyes while discussing reciprocal and nonreciprocal language. Wuyi Yuanlai places the boneless tongue beside eyes without sinews after telling the assembly that the displayed world is present yet still unseen. Tianru Weize answers by opposing sinews in the eyes to a tongue without bone, setting visual steadiness against verbal flexibility. Zhangxue Zui gives 'the tongue has no bone' as an answer to the third of Linji's four selections, then answers the fourth with the mouth as the gate of calamity. Xisou Shaotan admits his own boneless tongue while adding words to earlier teachers and calls the move a dog's tail joined to sable. Chushi Fanqi offers the phrase as one of several substitute answers. The saying therefore describes a capacity whose value depends on its use, not a fixed compliment.

Senses.Explanation: The term names a verse composed on an old case, the genre formed by such verses, and the act of composing them. Guan Youwudang calls Xuedou Chongxian's hundred verses essential study material and names Yuanwu Keqin's appraisal of Xuedou's old-case verses. Puhui places verses on old cases beside picking up old cases as distinct literary activities. Lingshu Sengyuan says one hundred such verses formed a book. Dahui Zonggao describes participants presenting interpretations and composing old-case verses. Biographical narratives say Zhengdang Mingbian composed one hundred in retirement and Dahui composed one hundred and ten while living at Yunmen Hermitage. Count, title, compilation, and composition grammar all point to the same literary product and activity; noun and verb frames do not require separate senses.
